intent: Stage A of ADR 0013: signed archives (Ed25519 signature over a fixed statement stored as OCI manifest annotations; keygen; trainer signs; Go and Java verify; run re-verifies; opt-in via public keys)
Slice 1: the signed statement and a frozen cross-language test vector

title: Sign a fixed line-based text, not JSON
why: A signature covers exact bytes, so both implementations must produce identical bytes. A fixed header, fixed field order and one 'name: value' per line has exactly one possible representation. JSON would need canonicalisation (key order, whitespace, number and string escaping), and two implementations disagreeing on one byte makes every signature fail to verify on the other side.
alternative: Sign a JSON document — rejected: canonical JSON is easy to get subtly different between Java and Go

title: Refuse a bad field instead of cleaning it
why: Every field is checked against a strict pattern (lowercase sha256 digests, a positive size, a repository path) and rejected otherwise. Because the text is one field per line, a newline inside a field could smuggle in a second line such as 'size: 1' and change what is signed. Refusing makes the framing unambiguous. Both languages must agree on strictness: Java uses matches() and Go uses an anchored pattern, so a trailing newline is refused in both (tested).
alternative: Escape or strip special characters — rejected: two escaping schemes would have to agree forever, and a silently altered field could verify against the wrong archive

title: Freeze one test vector, written once, that both languages must reproduce
why: If each side tested against its own expectations, they could drift apart and both suites stay green while archives signed by one fail on the other. The vector (fixed key, fixed fields, expected text and signature) was generated once by Go and is committed; Java must reproduce the same text and the same signature bytes. Ed25519 signing is deterministic, so exact equality is a valid test. The key is the published RFC 8032 test key, so committing it protects nothing and leaks nothing.
alternative: Each language tests only itself — rejected: it cannot detect the two sides disagreeing

name: SignedStatement / signedStatement
role: The exact text an archive signature covers: header, fingerprint, manifest digest, archive digest, size, repository, one per line
conditions: A verifier rebuilds it from what it observed and never reads it from the registry. The registry host is deliberately not included, because trainer and pods may reach one registry under different names. Same bytes in Java and Go.

name: vector.json
role: Frozen cross-language contract: key, fields, expected statement text and Ed25519 signature
conditions: Written once by Go, reproduced by Java. Change it only when the statement format changes, and then change both sides.

subject: Go's $ and Java's matches()
why: Both reject a trailing newline in a field only because the Go pattern is anchored with $ (strict end of text in Go's regexp) and Java uses matches(); a Perl-style $ would accept 'team/app\n' and let a field smuggle a line break. Tested on both sides.

subject: Ed25519 is deterministic
why: The same key and message always give the same signature, which is why the test can compare exact signature bytes across languages; randomised schemes (such as ECDSA) could not be tested this way.

intent: Slice 2: signing keys, the verifier and keygen

title: The key file stores both halves and checks they belong together
why: The JDK can sign with a private key but has no way to derive the public key from it, and a signature's key id comes from the public key. So the file keeps the seed and the public key, and loading signs a test message and verifies it with the public key; a mismatch is refused. That also catches a hand-edited or half-copied file before it can sign anything.
alternative: Store only the seed and derive the public key — rejected: not possible with the JDK's own Ed25519, and adding a library would break the no-dependencies rule

title: A public key is listed as id=base64, and the id must be that key's own id
why: The id is the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 of the public key. Pods are given 'id=base64' entries. An entry whose id is not the id of its key is skipped with a note, so a typo or a pasted-wrong key can never be trusted under a label that looks right, and a bad entry never stops an application. Skipping means that archive falls back to a miss, which is the safe outcome.
alternative: Trust whatever key the entry holds and ignore the id — rejected: a mislabelled key would silently be trusted, and rotation diagnostics would be unreadable

title: keygen creates the private file owner-only from the start and never overwrites
why: Creating a file and then tightening its permissions leaves a moment when others could read it, so the file is created already as rw-------. It refuses to overwrite an existing file, because overwriting a key you still need is unrecoverable and a replaced key makes every archive signed by the old one stop verifying. The seed is never printed; only the public half is.
alternative: Write then chmod, or print the key to the terminal — rejected: a window of exposure, and terminal output ends up in scrollback and logs

name: SigningKey
role: An Ed25519 key pair with a text file form (header, key id, public key, seed) and a signing method
conditions: Loading verifies the halves belong together. keyId is the first 8 bytes of SHA-256 of the raw public key. toString never shows the seed.

name: ArchiveVerifier
role: Answers VALID, UNKNOWN_KEY or BAD_SIGNATURE for a statement and a signature, against the listed public keys
conditions: Several keys can be listed for rotation. Malformed or mislabelled entries are skipped with a note. No usable key means nothing is checked (the opt-in default).

subject: A signature names its key by id, but the id proves nothing
why: A forger can put a trusted key's id on their own signature. Safety comes from the listed public key actually verifying the signature, not from the id matching; the test 'a stranger's signature under a trusted key id is bad' covers it.

intent: Slice 3: the store signs and verifies, the fetcher keeps the evidence

title: A key list in which nothing is usable refuses every archive
why: Turning checking on is done by setting a list of public keys. If the list is set but every entry is bad (a typo, a truncated paste), there are two ways to react: treat it as 'no list' and accept unsigned archives, or treat it as 'a list that trusts nothing' and refuse everything. The first silently switches protection off exactly when the operator tried to switch it on. The second costs only a cache, because a refused archive is a miss and the pod starts normally (constitution §1).
alternative: Ignore an unusable list and accept archives on digests alone — rejected: a typo would disable the protection without anyone noticing

title: An entry the trainer's own key did not sign counts as incomplete, so it is re-published
why: The trainer skips training when the store already has a complete entry for the fingerprint. If an unsigned or old-key entry counted as complete, switching signing on, or rotating to a new key, would change nothing: every existing archive would stay unsigned forever and pods that require signatures would never get a cache. Treating 'not signed by my key' as broken reuses the existing repair path, which re-publishes under the same tag.
alternative: Count any existing entry as complete — rejected: the first rollout and every rotation would silently do nothing

title: A trainer asked to sign refuses to publish unsigned
why: Everything on the pod start path fails open, so a problem never stops an application (constitution §3). The trainer is not on that path: it runs in its own job. If its key file is missing or corrupt and it carried on, it would publish unsigned archives while the operator believes signing is on, and pods that require signatures would just never get a cache with nothing pointing at why. Failing the job makes the problem visible, and no pod is affected because it keeps using whatever was already published.
alternative: Log and publish unsigned anyway (fail open) — rejected: it hides the misconfiguration and defeats the point of signing

name: OciArchiveStore signing
role: put signs and writes two manifest annotations; get and inspect rebuild the statement from the observed values and verify it
conditions: The statement uses the fingerprint asked for, the digest of the manifest blob that was just verified, the declared archive digest and size, and this repository. get verifies before the archive is downloaded, so a refused archive costs only the small manifest requests. A store with no verifier accepts signed and unsigned archives alike.

name: SignatureFile and the fetcher
role: mnemo-warmup.signature keeps the key id, signature and repository next to the archive, so run can check the files on disk again
conditions: The manifest is written byte for byte as the registry served it, because a signature covers those bytes. The signature file is written before the flags file, which stays the commit point; a miss withdraws all three.

subject: Tests that pass on the first run
why: The new signing tests all passed immediately, so the check that they can fail was made: with the verification line disabled, 8 of 11 failed. A security test that cannot fail proves nothing.

intent: Slice 4: run checks the signature on the files on disk

title: run checks the signature again from the files on disk at every start
why: fetch verified the archive when it downloaded it, but the cache directory is shared inside the pod and is writable by other processes, so what fetch checked is not what run is about to hand to the JVM. Checking again at start closes the gap between 'verified once' and 'used'. File permissions alone are not a defence here: the directory is typically open to every container that mounts it and processes often share a user. A signature does not depend on who can write: an attacker can swap the files but cannot make a valid signature for the swap.
alternative: Rely on fetch's check plus file modes — rejected: a swap after fetch would be used, and modes are easy to get wrong in a shared volume

title: The statement includes the SHA-256 of the manifest file's exact bytes
why: The manifest decides what the archive is valid for, and the planner trusts it. If the signature covered only a parsed field such as the fingerprint, an attacker could rewrite the rest of the file (JDK, flags, classpath) and keep a valid signature. Signing the digest of the file's bytes means any change to the file, even one that means nothing to the parser, breaks the signature. That also forced the Java fetch to write the downloaded bytes unchanged instead of re-serialising the parsed manifest.
alternative: Sign the parsed fingerprint only — rejected: it leaves the rest of the manifest editable under a valid signature

title: A signature problem at start is a plain start with the reason, never an error
why: run is on the application's start path. An untrusted, missing, unreadable or mismatched signature means we cannot vouch for the archive, so the JVM starts without it and the log says why. The application always starts (constitution §1 and §3). The only cost of a refused archive is a slower start.
alternative: Fail the container when a signature does not verify — rejected: a cache problem would become an outage

name: RunPlanner signature check
role: After the archive hash matches its manifest, rebuilds the signed statement from the files on disk and requires a trusted valid signature when public keys are configured
conditions: Uses the archive SHA-256 the planner already computes, the SHA-256 of the manifest file's bytes, the archive size, and the repository named in mnemo-warmup.signature. No key list means no check (opt-in). A list with nothing usable refuses everything.

subject: Hash checks and a signature protect against different attackers
why: A digest check only proves files agree with each other, so someone who can write the directory can swap the archive and rewrite the manifest to match. The test that does exactly that passes every digest check and is stopped only by the signature.

intent: Slice 5: the Go launcher verifies like Java does

title: An untrusted archive is skipped, not treated as a registry failure
why: The Go fetch used to end the whole lookup on any registry error. An archive that exists but is unsigned or signed by the wrong key is not the registry misbehaving: another cache type may be perfectly usable (on a newer JDK the fetch tries the AOT archive first, then AppCDS). A distinct 'untrusted' outcome moves on to the next candidate, exactly as the Java fetch does, and only if every candidate is refused does the fetch report why and start the pod without a cache.
alternative: Return the first refusal as a final error — rejected: it would make Go and Java behave differently for the same registry, and it could skip a perfectly good AppCDS archive

title: A failed signature check in the Go planner is handed to the Java planner
why: The Go planner exists to skip starting a JVM, and its rule is that it only ever answers 'use the archive' (every check passed) or 'nothing was fetched'. For anything else it passes the decision to the Java planner, which does the full set of checks and writes the reason in the log. The signature check follows the rule: Go can say yes only when it fully verified, and on any doubt Java repeats the check and explains. The refused case is rare and a slower start there is fine.
alternative: Let Go decide a plain start itself and write its own reason — rejected: a second copy of every reason message to keep in step with Java, for the rare path

title: The signature is saved with the archive even when nothing is enforced
why: A pod without a key list accepts any archive, but if the trainer signed it the fetch still writes mnemo-warmup.signature. That way an operator can turn checking on later, or a run given keys, and find the evidence already there, with no refetch. It is written before the flags file, which stays the last file written, so run never sees flags without the matching signature.
alternative: Write the signature file only when keys are configured — rejected: switching checking on would need a new fetch before it could work

name: launcher/signing.go
role: Go side of signed archives: the statement, key id, trusted-key list, verification and the signature file
conditions: Same rules and messages as ArchiveVerifier and SignatureFile; the frozen vector pins statement text, signature, key id and signature-file text for both languages.

name: native fetch and planner
role: Fetch verifies before requesting the archive and writes the signature file; the planner rebuilds the statement from the files on disk
conditions: An unusable key list refuses everything. The planner hands any failed check to Java.

subject: Base64 padding differs between the languages
why: Java's decoder accepts unpadded base64 and Go's requires padding. Files are always written padded. The mismatch can only make Go refuse a hand-edited unpadded file, which is a miss, the safe direction; it can never make Go accept something Java would refuse.

intent: Slice 6: wiring, documentation and the live proof

title: A typo in the key list is an error at preview, not a key that trusts nothing
why: The list of public keys is a string an operator pastes into an annotation. A pod that is given a list in which nothing parses refuses every archive, which is safe but silent: the cache just never works. So the injector runs the very parser the pods use when it reads the annotation, and any entry that does not parse, or whose id is not its key's own id, stops the preview with a message. The mistake is found at the desk, with the exact reason, instead of in production as a cache that never turns on.
alternative: Pass the string through and let each pod complain in its log — rejected: the failure is silent for the operator and shows up only after a rollout

title: The private key reaches the trainer only, and the preview says what that does not protect
why: The public keys go to the fetch and application containers, which only check. The private key is mounted into the trainer alone, read-only, with mode 0400, and appears nowhere in the application pod; a test searches the pod spec for it. But in stage A the trainer container also runs the application's code, so that code can read the key. The preview prints this limit next to the key ids so nobody mistakes stage A for full protection; stage B (splitting the trainer pod) removes it.
alternative: Say nothing about the limit and let the documentation carry it — rejected: a protection that looks bigger than it is does harm, so the warning goes where the operator reads it

title: The injector records the env names it owns, so a signed workload restores exactly
why: The injector writes a marker so it can undo its own changes, and it only removes what it recorded. Adding the key list to the application's env meant the old fixed list (just the cache directory) was no longer the whole truth. The marker now stores the names of the variables it added and restore uses them; a marker written before signing existed has none and falls back to the old list, so existing deployments still restore. Switching signing off removes the variable and nothing the application owns.
alternative: Hard-code both names in restore — rejected: it would try to remove a variable an older injection never added, and break restoring older workloads

title: The kind scenario tells the real rollout story and runs in both delivery modes
why: Unit tests prove each rule; only a cluster proves the pieces connect. The scenario starts with an unsigned archive in use, turns signing on and checks that the unsigned archive is refused while the pod still starts, lets the trainer re-publish it signed, checks that the pod then uses it and that the application container has no private key, and finally gives the pods the wrong public key and checks that they refuse it and still start. It runs in default mode (Java fetch and planner) and image-volume mode (the Go launcher), because the two verify with different code.
alternative: Test only the happy path with signing on — rejected: it would not show the first-rollout behaviour, which is where operators will actually be

name: signing annotations and chart values
role: signing-public-keys (pods) and signing-key-secret (trainer) in the injector; signing.publicKeys and signing.keySecret in the chart
conditions: Keys go to fetch and the application container; the private key is mounted 0400 into the trainer only. Nothing is rendered when signing is off.

name: e2e-kind WITH_SIGNING
role: Live proof on kind of the first rollout, the signed path and the wrong-key refusal
conditions: Makes keys with the example image's JDK, needs no Java on the host. Run it in both TOOLS_DELIVERY modes.

subject: Stage A is not the whole fix
why: The trainer container that holds the signing key also runs the application's code, so a compromised dependency could read the key. Documentation, the preview and this journal all say so; stage B (splitting the trainer pod) is the real separation.

intent: Review: fixes for the independent review of PR 148

title: A variable that is present enforces, even when blank
why: Raised in review: I had treated a blank key list as 'not set', so an empty value from a template or a typo silently turned verification off, which contradicts the rule that a typo must never switch protection off. A present variable now enforces: a list with nothing usable trusts nothing, every archive is a miss, and the log says so. The cost is only a cache. An absent variable still means signing is not in use.
alternative: Treat blank as absent — rejected: it is the failure the rule exists to prevent

title: Reject small-order and non-canonical public keys in both languages
why: Raised in review and reproduced: with the Ed25519 identity point listed as a trusted key, a trivial signature verified for any message in both the JDK and Go, and a non-canonical spelling of that key was accepted by Go and rejected by the JDK. No honest key looks like these, so both parsers refuse the five small-order points, their sign-bit variants and any y at or above p, using one list computed from the curve equation and pinned by the shared vector. Generated keys are never affected.
alternative: Trust whatever the operator lists — rejected: it let one mistaken or malicious entry defeat the check, and made Go and Java disagree

title: The key file is 0440 and the pod must give the trainer's user a group
why: Raised in review: Secret files are owned by root, so with mode 0400 a non-root trainer could not read the key at all, and inside the trainer container our tool and the application run as the same user, so 0400 never kept the application out either. 0440 lets the trainer read it through an fsGroup. A trainer known to be non-root without an fsGroup is refused at preview and at helm render with the fix named; when the image decides the user there is a note; an unreadable key fails the trainer with a permission-denied message that names fsGroup and publishes nothing.
alternative: 0444, simpler but world-readable inside the pod; or leaving 0400 and breaking non-root images

title: The trainer accepts anything the pods trust, and refuses to sign with a key they do not list
why: Raised in review: with each trainer checking only its own key, two trainers sharing a repository (one per cluster, say) treated each other's valid entries as broken and overwrote them alternately. The trainer now gets the pods' list and counts an entry as complete if any listed key signed it. In a rotation the entry keeps the old key's signature until the old key leaves the list, then the trainer re-publishes it. A trainer whose own key is not on the list would publish archives every pod refuses, so it stops with an error.
alternative: Each trainer trusts only its own key — rejected: alternating overwrites and pods losing the cache

title: The registry host stays out of the signed text; the replay is stated, not hidden
why: Raised in review. The trainer and the pods may reach one registry under different names (a mirror), so only the repository path is signed. The consequence is that a signed archive copied to another registry under the same repository path verifies there. That is documented plainly, with the guidance that registries that are different trust domains need separate keys, instead of claiming that moving an archive anywhere is rejected.
alternative: Bind the registry host — rejected: it breaks mirrors and any setup where the trainer and pods use different registry names

title: The check narrows the swap window; it does not claim to close it against a writer
why: Raised in review and correct: run hashes and verifies the archive by path and the JVM opens it a moment later, so a process that can write to the same volume can swap the file in between. The documentation no longer claims the directory is tamper-evident against an active writer. It says run detects changes made between fetch and start, recommends read-only mounts for consumers, and says that protects only against writes through that mount: another container or process with write access to the same volume can still race the JVM open.
alternative: Keep the claim — rejected: it would give false assurance. A real fix would hand the open file to the JVM, which is out of scope

name: Review fixes
role: Weak keys, present-but-blank values, bounded reads of cache files, CRLF parity, 0440 key file with fsGroup, trainer trusted list
conditions: All are covered by tests in both languages. The live scenario adds a non-root trainer and a key rotation.

subject: A review found what I tested for and missed what I assumed
why: My own tests asserted that a blank key list means 'no list', and my claims said the cache directory was tamper-evident. An independent reviewer questioned both, and both were wrong. The weak-key and replay claims were verified by running them, not by reading.
